To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

higher levels of maternal behavioral control predicted decreases in adolescent peer rejection and friends' deviant behavior from Time 1 to Time 2 at relatively low physiological arousal levels (i.e., lower skin conductance reactivity and greater respiratory sinus arrhythmias augmentation) and that these associations were stronger among boys.
higher levels of parental management of peers were related to better adolescent peer adjustment at lower levels of autonomic reactivity.

Parental management of peers via parental directing of youths’ peer interactions was associated with decreases over time in adolescents’ peer rejection and friends deviant behavior when youth exhibited low sympathetic nervous system (SNS) reactivity to challenge, as indicated by skin conductance level (i.e., SCL) reactivity, and high vagal tone, as indicated by respiratory sinus arrhythmias (i.e., RSA).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of physiological arousal in the association between parental management and peer outcomes.
the role of the autonomic nervous system in the development of adolescent peer adjustment.
the interplay of parental management of peers and physiological arousal in the development of adolescent peer relationships.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of the study are not consistent with the hypothesis that parental management of peers is associated with adolescent peer adjustment.
parental management of peers, particularly directing, is beneficial for youth, but only when they are not physiologically aroused.
parental management of peers is associated with better adolescent adjustment, but only for youth with relatively low physiological arousal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
parental directing of adolescents’ friendships is associated with positive changes in peer relationships among adolescents who exhibit relatively low arousal, but not among those with high arousal.
parents who are actively involved in their child’s social life and who are able to manage their child’s friendships are more likely to have children who have better peer relations.
parents can help to buffer the negative effects of peer deviancy on adolescents, but only when the adolescents are not over-aroused.
The main takeaway from our work is that
parental management of peers can be beneficial for youth with low arousal, but may have the opposite effect on adolescents who exhibit high levels of arousal.
parents should be mindful of how their management of peers is perceived by their children.
parental directing of adolescents’ peers may be beneficial for adolescents who are not overly responsive to challenge (e.g., low SCL or RSA reactivity).
